title: Social Security Checks to Rise 3.6% in 2027, With Biggest Dollar Gains in New Jersey and Connecticut - BigGo Finance
text:
Social Security Checks to Rise 3.6% in 2027, With Biggest Dollar Gains in New Jersey and Connecticut — BigGo Finance Ask AI News Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers More Ask AI News Watchlist Holdings Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Podcasts Influencers Social Security Checks to Rise 3.6% in 2027, With Biggest Dollar Gains in New Jersey and Connecticut
 Add preferred source Social Security benefits will rise 3.6% in 2027, up from 2.8% this year and above the decade's 3.4% average. The Social Security Administration expects the average retired-worker check to climb to $2,170 a month from $2,095, about $75 more monthly or $900 annually. Because the adjustment is a flat percentage, the largest dollar increases go to retirees with bigger underlying benefits, concentrated in states with high median payments led by New Jersey at $2,256 and Connecticut at $2,249. Residence does not affect benefit size directly; lifetime earnings and claiming age do. Agency data put the average benefit at age 67 at $2,016.48 and at age 70 at $2,274.68. Key Elements 
 Social Security Administration Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) New Jersey Connecticut Delaware New Hampshire Maryland Washington Michigan Minnesota Massachusetts Utah Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment will lift benefits by 3.6% in 2027, a bigger raise than recipients received this year and one that will translate into the largest dollar gains for retirees in a handful of high-income states.
 The increase compares with a 2.8% adjustment in 2026 and edges past the 3.4% average of the past decade. Because the adjustment is applied as a uniform percentage, every beneficiary receives the same rate, but the dollar amounts diverge sharply depending on the size of a retiree's underlying check.
 According to the Social Security Administration, the average monthly benefit for a retired worker will climb to $2,170 from $2,095, a gain of about $75 a month, or roughly $900 over the course of the year. The agency counts nearly 72 million beneficiaries in total, more than 55 million of them retirees.
 The adjustment is set by comparing the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W, for July through September of the current year with the same three months a year earlier. The resulting percentage becomes the following year's COLA.
 Where the dollars land hardest
 A retiree's state of residence has no direct bearing on benefit amounts, but it correlates with them. Payments are driven mainly by lifetime earnings and the age at which a worker claims, so states with higher median household incomes tend to post higher median benefits. The Social Security Administration's 2026 Annual Statistical Supplement ranks the states this way, based on December 2025 data:
 State Median monthly benefit for retired workers 
 New Jersey $2,256 
 Connecticut $2,249 
 Delaware $2,225 
 New Hampshire $2,215 
 Maryland $2,181 
 Washington $2,144 
 Michigan $2,139 
 Minnesota $2,135 
 Massachusetts $2,121 
 Utah $2,090 
 Note: Figures reflect median Social Security benefits for retired workers as of December 2025.
 Six of those states -- New Jersey, New Hampshire, Maryland, Washington, Massachusetts and Utah -- sit among the ten with the highest median household income, according to Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis data. Connecticut, Delaware and Minnesota all exceed the national median.
 Michigan is the outlier. Its median household income trails the national figure, yet its median Social Security benefit ranks in the top ten. That pattern could reflect a larger share of workers claiming at older ages, which raises monthly payments, or higher earners choosing to retire there.
 The practical takeaway is that relocating does not by itself raise a monthly check. States with larger average benefits generally have better-paid workforces, shaped by local labor markets and living costs, and those earnings histories follow workers into retirement.
 Claiming age and the earnings test
 Separate agency data show the average benefit for a 67-year-old at $2,016.48 a month as of December 2025, a figure that spans men at $2,234.41 and women at $1,801.82 -- a gap of $432.59. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, and it is the point at which a worker can collect an unreduced amount.
 Waiting beyond that age adds delayed retirement credits worth 8% a year up to age 70. For someone whose full retirement age is 67, those three additional years produce a 24% larger monthly check. The average benefit at age 70 stands at $2,274.68, or $258.20 above the age-67 figure.
 Claiming early carries a second cost for those still working. Under the retirement earnings test, a beneficiary under full retirement age for all of 2027 forfeits $1 of benefits for every $2 earned above $25,960. In the year a worker reaches full retirement age, the threshold rises to $67,920 and the withholding rate softens to $1 for every $3. Withheld amounts are restored through a higher benefit once full retirement age arrives.
 Social Security was designed to replace roughly 40% of pre-retirement wages, leaving most retirees dependent on savings or other income to cover total costs. The 2027 adjustment will add about $73 a month to the age-67 average.
 What it means for households
 The 3.6% raise offers only partial insulation from inflation, since it is calibrated to price changes already recorded rather than those ahead. For retirees whose spending skews toward health care and housing, the fit between the formula and actual costs can be loose.
 For near-retirees, the numbers argue for attention to timing rather than geography. Claiming strategy and earnings history move a monthly check far more than a change of address, and the gap between the age-67 and age-70 averages illustrates how much three years of patience is worth.
